robotics-controls-13-gyro-bias-drift.essentialQuestion: How does a tiny stationary gyroscope offset accumulate into a large reported heading change?
robotics-controls-13-gyro-bias-drift.verifiedBoundary: For fixed additive rate bias b, integrated yaw error after elapsed time T is bT; calibration only removes the estimated bias, not time-varying drift.
robotics-controls-13-gyro-bias-drift.analogy: Engineering interpretation: a plausible zero-rate sensor output is not proof of actual turning

starter.plainStart: For fixed additive rate bias b, integrated yaw error after elapsed time T is bT; calibration only removes the estimated bias, not time-varying drift.
starter.tryThis: Implement integrateYaw(rateDegPerSec,dt,n) for 600 constant +0.5°/s samples at dt=0.1 s; assert reported change +30°, actual change 0°.
starter.helper: Keep degrees and seconds consistent; do not accidentally treat degrees per second as radians per second.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Single-axis static gyro, exact uniform sampling, constant bias, perfect timebase; stochastic drift and temperature effects omitted. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/hardware/sensors/gyros-hardware.html
technical.versionCaution: The cited reference establishes background concepts, not independent authorization to operate hardware. No real robot actuation, deployment, or safety certification is implied.

reasoningSteps: Specify a stationary synthetic robot, actual yaw rate 0°/s, gyro measurement +0.50°/s, sample interval dt=0.10 s and total interval T=60.0 s (600 samples).
Forward rectangle integration gives 600*(0.50°/s)*(0.10 s)=+30.0° spurious heading change despite zero true rotation.
Independent continuous-time check integrates the constant bias: integral_0^60 0.50°/s dt = 30.0°; the discrete and continuous answers coincide for this constant input.
With stationary calibration samples [+0.40,+0.50,+0.60]°/s, the mean bias estimate is +0.50°/s; subtracting it from a subsequent +0.50°/s reading produces 0.00°/s corrected rate.

Counterexample: if true rotation is +10°/s while the sensor reads +10.50°/s, naively declaring every measured rate to be bias discards real motion. Zero-rate calibration requires a known stationary interval.
Recompute at T=120 s to predict 60° error, and at bias -0.25°/s for T=60 s to predict -15° error. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/hardware/sensors/gyros-hardware.html

robotics-controls-14-wrapped-yaw-innovat.essentialQuestion: Why must heading-fusion residuals wrap at the -180°/+180° boundary?
robotics-controls-14-wrapped-yaw-innovat.verifiedBoundary: For a periodic heading, innovation is wrap(observed-predicted) in [-180°,180°), not an ordinary arithmetic difference; fusion must respect equivalence modulo 360°.
robotics-controls-14-wrapped-yaw-innovat.analogy: Engineering interpretation: compass angles 179° and -179° are only 2° apart

starter.plainStart: For a periodic heading, innovation is wrap(observed-predicted) in [-180°,180°), not an ordinary arithmetic difference; fusion must respect equivalence modulo 360°.
starter.helper: Normalize only angular differences, then normalize the resulting heading if desired; never average raw signed angles across the branch cut.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Ideal 2D yaw values in degrees with exact sensor timestamps, scalar correction gain and no circular multimodality. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/pidcontroller.html

Apply predicted yaw plus gain times wrapped innovation: 179°+0.10*(+2°)=+179.2°; this is equivalent to -180.8° but +179.2° lies in [-180°,180°).
Independent unit-circle check gives signed relative angle atan2(sin(-358°),cos(-358°))=+2°; the same correction follows from the shortest rotation.
Counterexample: raw linear interpolation (0.90*179°+0.10*(-179°))=+143.2° creates a false 35.8° correction instead of +0.2°.

robotics-controls-15-two-anchor-range-am.essentialQuestion: Why do two ideal distance measurements sometimes fail to determine a unique planar robot position?
robotics-controls-15-two-anchor-range-am.verifiedBoundary: Two circle ranges to distinct known anchors generally intersect in zero, one or two planar points; an additional independent geometric constraint resolves a reflection ambiguity.
robotics-controls-15-two-anchor-range-am.analogy: Engineering interpretation: a distance to each of two posts does not reveal which side of the baseline a robot occupies

starter.helper: Derive circle-intersection coordinates before selecting a branch; a numerical fit alone does not prove identifiability.

robotics-controls-16-first-order-sensor-.essentialQuestion: How do sampling choices change a first-order robot sensor filter's response?
robotics-controls-16-first-order-sensor-.verifiedBoundary: Exponential discretization uses alpha=1-exp(-dt/tau), while implicit Euler uses alpha=dt/(tau+dt); both are stable for positive dt and tau but give different finite-step outputs.
robotics-controls-16-first-order-sensor-.analogy: Engineering interpretation: a smooth-looking signal can still be significantly delayed

starter.plainStart: Exponential discretization uses alpha=1-exp(-dt/tau), while implicit Euler uses alpha=dt/(tau+dt); both are stable for positive dt and tau but give different finite-step outputs.
starter.tryThis: Implement both alpha formulas for tau=0.40 s and dt=0.10 s; assert 0.2211992169 versus 0.2, keeping coefficients separate.

robotics-controls-17-actuator-command-sl.essentialQuestion: How can a rate limit bound the step-to-step change of a simulated drive velocity command?
robotics-controls-17-actuator-command-sl.verifiedBoundary: Rate-limited command recursion clips each requested change to ±a_max*dt; it limits the command signal, not actual acceleration or stopping distance.
robotics-controls-17-actuator-command-sl.analogy: Engineering interpretation: smoothing a command is not a measurement that the mechanism followed it

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Dimensionally consistent synthetic velocity-command stream with fixed sample period, symmetric rate limit and no plant dynamics. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/filters/slew-rate-limiter.html
technical.versionCaution: The cited reference establishes background concepts, not independent authorization to operate hardware. No real robot actuation, deployment, or safety certification is implied.

reasoningSteps: Let commanded translational speed start at v0=0 m/s, user-requested target be +1.00 m/s, sample interval dt=0.10 s and slew bound a_max=2.00 m/s².

Independent telescoping check: five increments of 0.20 m/s total 1.00 m/s, and every increment obeys |v[k+1]-v[k]|<=0.20 m/s.
For a new target -1.00 m/s from current +1.00 m/s, the next issued command is +0.80 m/s, not -1.00 m/s; ten 0.20-m/s decrements reach -1.00 m/s.

robotics-controls-18-pid-derivative-kick.essentialQuestion: Why can derivative-on-error produce a sudden controller command when only the setpoint changes?
robotics-controls-18-pid-derivative-kick.verifiedBoundary: Derivative-on-error differentiates both setpoint and measurement; derivative-on-measurement excludes the setpoint step but still responds to measurement noise.
robotics-controls-18-pid-derivative-kick.analogy: Engineering interpretation: changing the goal instantly does not mean the measured robot position moved instantly

starter.plainStart: Derivative-on-error differentiates both setpoint and measurement; derivative-on-measurement excludes the setpoint step but still responds to measurement noise.
starter.tryThis: Compute derivative-on-error and derivative-on-measurement at a 1 m setpoint jump and fixed 0 m measurement; assert respective terms +5 and 0 command units.
starter.helper: Write e=r-y and its difference before calculating the derivative; make the controlled variable's units explicit.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Synthetic discrete difference, constant gains and synchronized samples; plant dynamics, filtering, saturation and actuator noise omitted. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/pidcontroller.html
technical.versionCaution: The cited reference establishes background concepts, not independent authorization to operate hardware. No real robot actuation, deployment, or safety certification is implied.

reasoningSteps: Use sampled position control, measured position y0=y1=0 m, desired setpoint r0=0 m and r1=1.00 m, dt=0.020 s, derivative gain Kd=0.10 command*s/m.
Error changes from e0=0 to e1=+1.00 m; derivative-on-error reports (e1-e0)/dt=+50 m/s and produces a +5.0 normalized-command derivative term.
Derivative-on-measurement instead produces -Kd*(y1-y0)/dt=0 because the measured robot position did not move.
Independent difference identity confirms (e1-e0)/dt=(r1-r0)/dt-(y1-y0)/dt=50-0=50 m/s.
Counterexample: derivative-on-measurement is not noise-free; if the next measurement jumps by +0.010 m in 0.020 s at constant setpoint, derivative term becomes -0.050 normalized command.

Real controllers may filter derivatives, bound commands, or use setpoint trajectories; this exercise isolates the discrete derivative placement, not a universal PID tuning recommendation. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/pidcontroller.html

robotics-controls-19-one-sample-feedback.essentialQuestion: How can one sample of feedback delay destabilize an otherwise stable ideal P controller?
robotics-controls-19-one-sample-feedback.verifiedBoundary: For x[k+1]=x[k]+g(r-x[k-1]), the error characteristic polynomial is lambda²-lambda+g=0; asymptotic stability holds for 0<g<1, narrower than the no-delay 0<g<2 case.
robotics-controls-19-one-sample-feedback.analogy: Engineering interpretation: stale measurements can amplify an oscillation even when the gain is acceptable for a zero-delay model

starter.plainStart: For x[k+1]=x[k]+g(r-x[k-1]), the error characteristic polynomial is lambda²-lambda+g=0; asymptotic stability holds for 0<g<1, narrower than the no-delay 0<g<2 case.
starter.tryThis: Simulate ten steps for delayed recurrence using x[-1]=x0=0 and g=0.5; assert x1=0.5, x2=1, x3=1.25 and x4=1.25.
starter.helper: Derive the delayed two-state recurrence; a no-delay pole calculation is not valid for this plant.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Scalar unit-gain discrete integrator, exact one-sample feedback delay, constant reference, no saturation or nonlinear dynamics. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/pidcontroller.html
technical.versionCaution: The cited reference establishes background concepts, not independent authorization to operate hardware. No real robot actuation, deployment, or safety certification is implied.

reasoningSteps: Define dimensionless reference r=1, x[-1]=x[0]=0, sample time dt=0.10 s, Kp=5 s^-1, and g=dt*Kp=0.50.
Delayed control law x[k+1]=x[k]+g*(1-x[k-1]) yields x1=0.50, x2=1.00, x3=1.25, x4=1.25.
Writing e[k]=1-x[k] gives e[k+1]=e[k]-g*e[k-1], hence characteristic roots lambda=(1±sqrt(1-4g))/2; at g=0.5 roots (1±i)/2 have magnitude sqrt(0.5)=0.707106781.
Independent quadratic invariant: root product equals g; for complex-conjugate roots the squared magnitude is g, confirming decaying oscillations at g=0.5.
Counterexample: g=1.20 would satisfy the zero-delay requirement 0<g<2, yet delayed roots have modulus sqrt(1.20)=1.095445115>1, so generic disturbances grow rather than decay.

Border case g=1 has roots on the unit circle and is not asymptotically stable; extra physical sample delays or nonlinearities require a different model and analysis. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/pidcontroller.html

robotics-controls-20-watchdog-stop-latch.essentialQuestion: How can a synthetic heartbeat watchdog enforce a latched stop after a missed deadline?
robotics-controls-20-watchdog-stop-latch.verifiedBoundary: A deterministic state machine enters STOP_LATCHED if elapsed time since last heartbeat reaches the configured threshold at a polling event; a fresh heartbeat alone must not clear the latch.
robotics-controls-20-watchdog-stop-latch.analogy: Engineering interpretation: a recovered message cannot retroactively prove a fault never occurred

starter.plainStart: A deterministic state machine enters STOP_LATCHED if elapsed time since last heartbeat reaches the configured threshold at a polling event; a fresh heartbeat alone must not clear the latch.
starter.tryThis: Write an event reducer over integer-ms timestamps and states READY/STOP_LATCHED; assert READY at t=100 and STOP_LATCHED at t=120 after last heartbeat t=20.
starter.helper: Test exact threshold equality, heartbeat recovery, deliberate reset and monotonic timestamps separately.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Pure offline event automaton and abstract stop flag; not a hardware safety circuit, emergency-stop design or certified protective device. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/hardware-apis/motors/wpi-drive-classes.html
technical.versionCaution: The cited reference establishes background concepts, not independent authorization to operate hardware. No real robot actuation, deployment, or safety certification is implied.

reasoningSteps: Model states READY and STOP_LATCHED, heartbeat timestamp 20 ms, expiry threshold 100 ms and periodic polling at t=20,40,60,80,100,120 ms.
At t=100 ms elapsed time since last heartbeat is 80 ms; the state remains READY. At t=120 ms elapsed is 100 ms; predicate elapsed>=100 ms becomes true and state enters STOP_LATCHED.
Independent check using integer milliseconds evaluates time difference 120-20=100 ms and verifies the boundary exactly, without floating-point timer jitter.

At t=140 ms a post-timeout heartbeat updates lastHeartbeat but must leave STOP_LATCHED and the abstract stop flag active. Model two separate recovery predicates: a heartbeat received after the latch event and an independently declared faultsCleared flag. At t=141 ms, reset still fails without clearance; after a hypothetical faults-cleared event at t=142 ms, explicit reset at t=143 ms may return READY because the 140-ms heartbeat remains fresh (3<100 ms). In this model faultsCleared is a supplied assumption, never proof of a physical safety condition.

Counterexample: implementing heartbeat as automatic reset loses a latched fault; implementing reset whenever lastHeartbeat is recent ignores uncleared faults. An invalid event that advances lastEvent before event-type validation can also reject a later valid event at t=140 ms, so validation must precede all state mutation.

Actual motor safety systems also depend on wiring, command outputs, safety ratings, independent watchdog paths and real-time scheduling; this simulation establishes none of them. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/hardware-apis/motors/wpi-drive-classes.html

robotics-controls-21-swept-obstacle-inte.analogy: Engineering interpretation: two safe snapshots do not prove the motion between them was safe

robotics-controls-22-encoder-delta-quant.essentialQuestion: How does subtracting two quantized encoder positions change the displacement error bound?
robotics-controls-22-encoder-delta-quant.verifiedBoundary: With independently rounded absolute encoder positions, each endpoint has at most half-count quantization error, so their difference can err by nearly one whole count.
robotics-controls-22-encoder-delta-quant.analogy: Engineering interpretation: two imperfect position snapshots do not inherit the uncertainty bound of a single snapshot

starter.plainStart: With independently rounded absolute encoder positions, each endpoint has at most half-count quantization error, so their difference can err by nearly one whole count.
starter.tryThis: Calculate 2*pi*0.05/2048 m/count and the observed 100-count displacement; assert 0.015339807879 m.
starter.helper: Distinguish an absolute rounded position from a difference of two rounded positions.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Wheel-shaft cumulative encoder, nearest-integer rounding, effective resolution 2048 counts/revolution, radius 0.05 m, no slip or backlash. Reference: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/13-4-odometry/
technical.versionCaution: The cited reference establishes background concepts, not independent authorization to operate hardware. No real robot actuation, deployment, or safety certification is implied.

reasoningSteps: Let r=0.050 m and resolution N=2048 counts per wheel revolution; one count corresponds to s=2*pi*r/N=0.000153398079 m.
Observed absolute positions c0=100 and c1=200 counts yield displacement (200-100)*s=0.015339807879 m.
At each independent snapshot, nearest-count rounding gives an error no greater than 0.5 count; subtracting them gives a worst-case absolute difference error at most 1 count, or 0.000153398079 m.

Independent counterexample with true fractional positions 100.49 and 199.51 counts: rounding returns 100 and 200; actual difference is 99.02 counts but the reported difference is 100 counts, an error of +0.98 count.

Claiming a half-count bound for this difference fails the counterexample; a half-count bound applies to one quantized absolute position relative to a known exact reference, not two independently rounded endpoints.

Any wheel slip, missed transitions, unknown gear ratio, backlash or calibration error adds uncertainties not covered by this pure quantization calculation. Source: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/13-4-odometry/

robotics-controls-23-wheel-radius-asymme.essentialQuestion: How can a small left/right wheel-radius mismatch produce yaw during a nominally straight drive?
robotics-controls-23-wheel-radius-asymme.verifiedBoundary: In ideal differential-drive odometry, heading change is (right-travel-left-travel)/track; commanded equal wheel revolutions do not guarantee equal ground distances when effective radii differ.
robotics-controls-23-wheel-radius-asymme.analogy: Engineering interpretation: a straight motor command can produce a curved path even with perfect encoder counts

starter.plainStart: In ideal differential-drive odometry, heading change is (right-travel-left-travel)/track; commanded equal wheel revolutions do not guarantee equal ground distances when effective radii differ.
starter.tryThis: Compute dtheta for effective wheel distances dL=1.00, dR=1.02 m and b=0.50 m; assert +0.04 rad.
starter.helper: Use actual effective wheel travel for kinematics; encoder count equality is only a proxy when wheel radii are equal.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Planar two-wheel no-slip model, wheel distances supplied synthetically, constant-curvature segment; no real wheel measurements or friction effects. Reference: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/13-4-odometry/
technical.versionCaution: The cited reference establishes background concepts, not independent authorization to operate hardware. No real robot actuation, deployment, or safety certification is implied.

reasoningSteps: Set nominal expected wheel travel dL=dR=1.00 m and track b=0.50 m. Suppose synthetic unequal effective radius makes actual right travel 1.02 m while left remains 1.00 m.
Wheel-distance difference is 0.02 m, so yaw increment dtheta=(1.02-1.00)/0.50=+0.04 rad, approximately +2.291831°.
Center arc distance is ds=(1.00+1.02)/2=1.01 m. Its constant-curvature radius is R=ds/dtheta=25.25 m.
Independent integration gives dx=ds*sin(dtheta)/dtheta and dy=ds*(1-cos(dtheta))/dtheta; for +0.04 rad, dx≈1.009730688 m and dy≈0.020197307 m.
Counterexample: treating equal commanded motor revolutions as proof of dL=dR falsely predicts zero yaw and zero lateral drift, overlooking effective radius mismatch.

Reversing which side has 2% extra travel changes dtheta to -0.04 rad and reverses lateral drift sign. Wheel-ground slip would invalidate the neat radius-only attribution. Source: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/13-4-odometry/

robotics-controls-24-pose-covariance-rot.essentialQuestion: How must planar position uncertainty transform when a robot's coordinate frame rotates?
robotics-controls-24-pose-covariance-rot.verifiedBoundary: For a constant 2D rotation matrix R, covariance changes as P_new=R P_old R^T; the trace and eigenvalues are preserved, but axis-aligned variances need not be.
robotics-controls-24-pose-covariance-rot.analogy: Engineering interpretation: the same uncertainty ellipse looks different from rotated axes

starter.plainStart: For a constant 2D rotation matrix R, covariance changes as P_new=R P_old R^T; the trace and eigenvalues are preserved, but axis-aligned variances need not be.
starter.tryThis: Implement 2x2 covariance rotation with yaw=pi/2 and P=diag(0.04,0.01) m²; assert world diagonal [0.01,0.04] m² and off-diagonal approximately zero.
starter.helper: A covariance is not a point coordinate; translate the mean, but rotate covariance through matrix multiplication.

technical.scope: Synthetic, offline educational case. Static linear covariance transform of a synthetic planar random position, zero translation uncertainty and no cross-time correlations. Reference: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html
technical.versionCaution: The cited reference establishes background concepts, not independent authorization to operate hardware. No real robot actuation, deployment, or safety certification is implied.

reasoningSteps: Let a robot-local planar position error have covariance P_local=diag(0.04,0.01) m², with x and y standard deviations 0.20 m and 0.10 m.
For a world-from-local rotation yaw +90°, R=[[0,-1],[1,0]]. Transform covariance: P_world=R P_local R^T=diag(0.01,0.04) m².
Independent invariants give trace(P_local)=trace(P_world)=0.05 m² and determinant(P_local)=det(P_world)=0.0004 m^4; both confirm a rigid rotation preserved total scatter.
Adding a deterministic translation t=(2,3) m shifts the mean but leaves covariance unchanged, since cov(X+t)=cov(X).

Counterexample: copying P_local unchanged to world axes falsely reports world-x variance 0.04 m² rather than 0.01 m² after 90° rotation; the apparent uncertainty direction is wrong even though the trace matches.

At 180° both axis variances return to (0.04,0.01) m². The result does not apply directly to nonlinear transforms with correlated orientation uncertainty. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html
